<FromTheBinary topic="crud" />

An entity read in cyoda-go reads one of two things: the current committed
state, or the state **as at an instant** given in `pointInTime`. This page
covers when a read's answer is fixed, how to read "now" with an answer that
cannot change, how to page a list consistently, and what a read inside a
transaction sees.

The per-endpoint parameters are in
[working with entities](/build/working-with-entities/) and
[searching entities](/build/searching-entities/).

## Revisions are dated at commit

A revision is dated at the instant its transaction **commits**, on every
storage backend. It is not dated at the instant the transaction started, and
not at the instant the individual write was issued.

Every entity a transaction writes carries the same instant. Two entities
created by one collection create report the same `creationDate`:

```json
"2026-11-22T22:07:48.197162Z"
"2026-11-22T22:07:48.197162Z"
```

The server assigns both entity dates:

- `meta.creationDate` is the commit instant of the transaction that created
  the entity. Later updates do not change it.
- `meta.lastUpdateTime` is the commit instant of the transaction that wrote
  this revision.

A client cannot set either date. The server takes the instant immediately
before the commit, so a date you read back is at or before the moment the
write response returned, and never as early as the moment the transaction
opened.

Because one transaction has one instant, a `pointInTime` read sees all of a
transaction's writes or none of them.

## One version per entity per transaction

A transaction records **one** version of each entity it writes, however often
it writes that entity. A later write in the same transaction replaces the
pending version. This holds for a workflow whose processors and automatic
transitions write the entity several times, and for a collection update that
names the same entity twice:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/entity/JSON \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '[
    { "id": "'"$ENTITY_ID"'", "payload": "{\"orderId\":\"ORD-50\",\"amount\":110}" },
    { "id": "'"$ENTITY_ID"'", "payload": "{\"orderId\":\"ORD-50\",\"amount\":120}" }
  ]'
```

The entity's data is the second payload (`amount` `120`), and its change
history gains one `UPDATE` entry for the transaction. `GET /api/entity/{entityId}/changes` has
one entry for each transaction that changed the entity.

## Point-in-time reads

A read with `pointInTime` returns the state as at exactly that instant,
**inclusive**. A revision dated exactly at `pointInTime` is included, and the
server applies no rounding. The bound is compared at the storage engine's
native precision. Backends store timestamps at different precisions, so
results agree across backends at millisecond granularity.

These reads take `pointInTime`:

- `GET /api/entity/{entityId}` and the list `GET /api/entity/{entityName}/{modelVersion}`.
- Direct search, and async search submission.
- Conditional delete, `DELETE /api/entity/{entityName}/{modelVersion}`.
- The four `GET /api/entity/stats…` reads, and grouped statistics (as a body
  field).
- `GET /api/entity/{entityId}/changes` and `GET /api/entity/{entityId}/transitions`.

A point-in-time read is committed-only. Inside a transaction it ignores the
transaction's own uncommitted writes.

### RFC 3339, strictly

`pointInTime` is an RFC 3339 date-time with a time zone. The server reads it
strictly:

- Fractional seconds follow a `.`, at any precision up to nanoseconds.
- The hour has two digits.
- An offset such as `+02:00` is accepted and compared as the instant it names.
- A bare date (`2026-03-31`) and an empty value are refused.

A malformed query parameter is `400 BAD_REQUEST`, with the parameter named in
`properties.parameter`:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "BAD_REQUEST: invalid value for parameter 'pointInTime'",
  "instance": "/entity/orders/1",
  "properties": {
    "errorCode": "BAD_REQUEST",
    "parameter": "pointInTime"
  }
}
```

In the grouped-statistics body the same mistake is `400 MALFORMED_REQUEST`.

<Aside type="caution" title="Encode the offset">

A `+` in a query string decodes as a space, so
`?pointInTime=2026-03-31T23:59:59+01:00` is refused. Percent-encode it
(`%2B01:00`), let your HTTP client encode the parameter, or send the instant
in UTC with `Z`.

</Aside>

## The consistency time

A read at an instant is trustworthy only if no save can still land at or
before that instant. The **consistency time** is the latest instant for which
that holds, for your tenant. It is normally the store's current time. It
waits only for saves that are still committing, which takes milliseconds.

The consistency time has four properties:

- **Complete.** Every save already confirmed to any client, on any node, is at
  or before it.
- **Final.** A read at or before it sees every save of your tenant dated at or
  before that instant, and gives the same answer for ever. A save that is not
  yet dated when the consistency time is returned is dated after it.
- **Never goes back.** Each consistency time is at or after every one returned
  earlier, on any node, and across a restart.
- **Exact.** It is never rounded up, and it covers the store's own read
  resolution.

### `GET /api/entity/consistency-time`

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/api/entity/consistency-time \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```json
{"consistencyTime":"2026-11-22T22:05:35.03883Z"}
```

The value is at the store's full precision. Over gRPC the same value comes
from `EntityConsistencyTimeGetRequest`.

When [clock control](/help/clock/) is on, the store takes its time from the
platform clock, which a test can set.

### The fence

A read with a `pointInTime` later than the consistency time is refused with
`400 POINT_IN_TIME_AFTER_CONSISTENCY_TIME`. The server does not wait. The
problem carries the current consistency time in `properties.consistencyTime`:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "POINT_IN_TIME_AFTER_CONSISTENCY_TIME: pointInTime 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z is later than the consistency time 2026-11-22T22:08:34.85159Z; read at or before the consistency time (GET /entity/consistency-time returns the current one)",
  "instance": "/entity/orders/1",
  "properties": {
    "consistencyTime": "2026-11-22T22:08:34.85159Z",
    "errorCode": "POINT_IN_TIME_AFTER_CONSISTENCY_TIME"
  }
}
```

An instant at or before the store's clock is never refused this way: the
store waits for the tenant's saves that are still committing. Only an instant
later than the store's clock is refused. That is a future instant, or an
instant from a client clock that runs ahead of the store's clock. Over gRPC
the envelope has no properties, so the consistency time is in the message
text.

Errors that do not involve the instant are reported first: a malformed value,
an unknown model, or `pointInTime` together with `transactionId`. A `404` that
the read itself produces, such as an unknown entity id, comes after the fence.

`503 CONSISTENCY_TIME_UNAVAILABLE` (retryable) means the store could not
certify a consistency time within its wait budget, because a save stayed in
its commit phase too long. The budget is 10 seconds on PostgreSQL (or
`CYODA_POSTGRES_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT` when that is lower) and up to 11 seconds on
SQLite; the memory backend never waits. The response has no `Retry-After`
header. Retry with back-off, for example starting at 100 ms and doubling.
Repeated occurrences mean that a commit is stalling. The consistency-time
read, an async search submitted without `pointInTime`, and any read with a
`pointInTime` can answer it.

## Reading "now" with a fixed answer

A read without `pointInTime` reads what is committed when the store runs the
query. Two such reads can differ.

To read the current state with an answer that cannot change, take the
consistency time and pass it as `pointInTime`. A read at that value:

- is never refused with `POINT_IN_TIME_AFTER_CONSISTENCY_TIME`, on any node
  (a `503` is still possible);
- includes every save confirmed before you asked;
- returns the same answer if you repeat it.

Do not use the client's own clock for "now". A client clock that runs ahead
of the store's clock produces instants that the fence refuses.

## Consistent paging

The pages of a list read without `pointInTime` are read at different
moments. An entity created or deleted between two page requests can shift
the pages, so an entity can be skipped or returned twice.

For consistent pages, take the consistency time **once** and pass it as
`pointInTime` on every page:

```bash
BASE=http://localhost:8080/api
PAGE_SIZE=100
CT=$(curl -s "$BASE/entity/consistency-time" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -r .consistencyTime)

page=0
while :; do
  batch=$(curl -s --get "$BASE/entity/orders/1" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    --data-urlencode "pointInTime=$CT" \
    --data-urlencode "pageSize=$PAGE_SIZE" \
    --data-urlencode "pageNumber=$page")
  echo "$batch" | jq -c '.[]'
  [ "$(echo "$batch" | jq length)" -lt "$PAGE_SIZE" ] && break
  page=$((page + 1))
done
```

Every page reads the same state, on whichever node serves it, and each entity
carries the instant in `meta.pointInTime`. The list order is stable and
deterministic; the specific order depends on the storage engine and is based
on the entity id.

The same recipe makes a set of reads agree with each other: pass one
consistency time to a list, a search and a statistics query, and they
describe one state of the data.

## Async search

An async search submitted **without** `pointInTime` takes a fresh consistency
time at submission and records it on the job. The status and every result
page read at that instant, so all pages of the result agree. The result
includes every save already confirmed when the submit was made. A save that
is not yet confirmed at submission may or may not appear.

A `pointInTime` you pass is fenced at submission and recorded the same way.
See [async search](/build/searching-entities/#an-async-search).

## Reads inside a transaction

A compute node's callback that carries the transaction token
(`X-Tx-Token`) [joins the workflow's transaction](/build/client-compute-nodes/#1031-transaction-joined-callbacks).
A read on that callback runs inside the transaction:

- **Without `pointInTime`**, it sees the transaction's snapshot plus its own
  writes: the committed state as it was when the transaction began. A commit
  by another transaction that completes later is not visible to it, also when
  it reads again.
- **With `pointInTime`**, it sees committed data at that instant only, and it
  is fenced like any other point-in-time read.
- **Change history** lists committed changes only, on every backend. The
  transaction's own pending changes do not appear.

A search inside a transaction can also add the entities it returns to the
transaction's read-set. See
[searching inside a transaction](/build/searching-entities/#searching-inside-a-transaction).

## Reading what a transaction wrote

`GET /api/entity/{entityId}?transactionId={transactionId}` returns the
entity as that transaction left it: the one version the transaction
committed.

- It reads committed transactions only. A transaction that has not committed
  (also when the request itself joins it), never wrote the entity, or deleted
  it answers `404 ENTITY_NOT_FOUND`.
- `pointInTime` and `transactionId` together are `400 BAD_REQUEST`.

`GET /api/entity/{entityId}/transitions?transactionId={transactionId}`
resolves the transaction to its commit instant and lists the transitions
available at that instant. The instant is fenced like a `pointInTime`. Any
node can resolve it, also after a restart. It is kept for one hour after the
commit. An older id, an unknown id, or an id from another tenant is
`400 BAD_REQUEST`.
